by: session, Adrian's watch 18 Oct 2026 (explain why we start by subtracting)

beats.say: Call the pump's intensity I P. The pump is fifty decibels, so fifty equals ten log I P over K.
asks: Why is the pump fifty equals ten log I P over K?

beats.say: Call the dishwasher's intensity I D. It is sixty-two decibels, so sixty-two equals ten log I D over K.
We want the intensity of the dishwasher over the intensity of the pump. That is I D over I P.
asks: Why I D over I P and not I P over I D?

beats.say: But K is unknown. Subtracting the two equations joins the two logs into one, and K cancels.
asks: Why can't we find each intensity on its own?

beats.say: So take the dishwasher's equation minus the pump's: sixty-two minus fifty equals the two logs, one minus the other.
asks: Why the dishwasher minus the pump?

beats.say: Minus Power turns the right side into one log of the ratio. The K cancels.
asks: What is the Minus Power law?

beats.say: Divide both sides by ten. Log of the ratio is one point two.
Log is base ten, so un-log with ten to the power. The ratio is ten to the power one point two.
Ten to the power one point two is about fifteen point eight.
asks: How do I key this in?

beats.say: So the dishwasher is about fifteen point eight times as intense as the pump.
